vLeaf@DSSAT: leaf biochemistry inside CERES-Maize, tested from hours to harvest

Integrating two-leaf sun–shade photosynthesis and energy balance into CERES-Maize

Antriksh Srivastava · Centre of Studies in Resources Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Bombay · srivastava.antriksh96@gmail.com

AGU26 Annual Meeting, abstract B23F-2247 · San Francisco, 7–11 December 2026 · Version of 26 November 2026 (Drewry et al. leaf parameters; calibration cost: silking date + grain yield; surrogate designs seed 21 and 99)

Abstract

Crop models such as DSSAT CERES-Maize convert intercepted light to biomass with a daily radiation-use efficiency, so they cannot be tested against the half-hourly carbon and water fluxes that eddy-covariance towers measure. We replaced that one step with vLeaf, a two-leaf (sunlit/shaded) model of C4 photosynthesis, stomatal conductance and leaf energy balance that runs every hour, and left the rest of DSSAT unchanged. vLeaf used published maize leaf parameters and was never fitted; only five cultivar coefficients were calibrated, against silking date and grain yield alone, leaving one of four maize seasons at the AmeriFlux US-Bo1 site (Bondville, Illinois) out each time. In the seasons left out, the coupled model predicted leaf area with R2 = 0.79 (n = 60), daily gross primary production (GPP) with R2 = 0.66 (n = 374 days), daily evapotranspiration with R2 = 0.78 (n = 132 days), silking within 5 days and grain yield within −4 to +8 % of farmer records; leaf area, GPP and evapotranspiration were never used in fitting. Placing a biochemical leaf model inside a crop model makes the whole chain from hourly fluxes to yield testable, and here locates the main remaining error in leaf ageing after silking rather than in photosynthesis itself.

Key findings

  1. Every maize season was predicted by a model calibrated without it: leaf area R2 0.79, daily GPP R2 0.66, half-hourly GPP R2 0.64 (n = 7,826) and daily ET R2 0.78 (Table 4, Figure 3).
  2. Predicted silking fell within 5 days of the reference dates and grain yield within −4 to +8 % of farmer records (Table 4, Figure 4).
  3. Only five cultivar coefficients were fitted, to silking date and grain yield alone, and the four independent calibrations agreed closely, for example P1 210–228 °C d and G2 842–904 kernels per plant (Table 2). Of nine cost functions compared, silking and yield are the two observations the calibration needs; adding LAI or GPP to the cost did not improve held-out skill (Section 3.1, Table 6).
  4. The largest error is late-season GPP that stays too high because neither vLeaf nor CERES-Maize ages leaves correctly after silking; it is worst in 2003, where daily GPP R2 is 0.52 (Figure 3, Section 5).
  5. A surrogate trained on 10,000 DSSAT-vLeaf runs reproduces DSSAT on 1,000 independent runs (grain yield R2 0.979, silking R2 0.995) and powers the interactive season model in Section 4.1 (Appendix A).

1Introduction

CERES-Maize [1] turns intercepted light into biomass with one daily light-use efficiency. Leaves do not work that way: photosynthesis and transpiration respond within the hour to light, temperature, humidity and CO2, and that is the time scale at which eddy-covariance towers measure them. A crop model that computes hourly leaf gas exchange can therefore be tested at the tower's own time scale, not only against end-of-season yield.

Here we place the two-leaf model vLeaf inside DSSAT-CSM v4.8.5, change nothing else, and ask whether the coupled model can predict maize seasons it was never calibrated on, from half-hourly photosynthesis to leaf area, silking and grain yield.

2Methods

2.1Model and coupling

Every hour DSSAT passes vLeaf the weather, the leaf area index (LAI) and its water (SWFAC) and nitrogen (NSTRESS) stress factors (Figure 1). vLeaf splits the canopy into sunlit and shaded leaf area and the direct and diffuse light each absorbs [5, 6], gives each fraction a photosynthetic capacity integrated over canopy depth with leaf nitrogen declining exponentially (Eq. 1), and solves each leaf for C4 photosynthesis [3, 4] (Eq. 2), Ball–Berry stomatal conductance (Eqs. 3–4), boundary-layer conductance [8] and the leaf energy balance [8] (Eq. 5), iterating until leaf temperature, Ci, gs and An agree. Canopy GPP is the sum over the two leaf classes (Eq. 6). The daily sum of canopy carbon replaces the CERES-Maize carbon supply; phenology, leaf-area growth and senescence, partitioning, the soil water and nitrogen balance and grain formation remain CERES-Maize.

C4 photosynthesisAn=min(AcRub,AjRub,AcPEP,AjPEP)−Rd(2)
Stomatal conductancegs=b+mβSWAnhsCs−Γ(3)
Intercellular CO2Ci=Cs−1.6Angs(4)
Leaf energy balanceRn(Tleaf)=H(Tleaf)+λE(Tleaf)(5)
Canopy GPPGPP=(An+Rd)sunLAIsun+(An+Rd)shLAIsh(6)

In Eq. 1, kn = 0.5 is the leaf-nitrogen extinction coefficient and kb the direct-beam extinction coefficient; the integral is evaluated in closed form. In Eq. 3, b and m are the Ball–Berry intercept and slope, hs the relative humidity at the leaf surface, Γ the CO2 compensation point and βSW = SWFAC. Eq. 5 is solved for leaf temperature by a golden-section search.

2.2Site and data

AmeriFlux US-Bo1 at Bondville, Illinois (40.006° N, 88.292° W, 219 m) is a no-till maize–soybean rotation on Flanagan silt loam; maize was grown in 1999, 2001, 2003 and 2005 [10, 16]. Only measured data were used, with no gap-filling (Table 1). Two quality screens were applied. First, 2003 DOY 207–208 were dropped: their flux, flagged as measured, shows net CO2 release of up to 46 µmol m−2 s−1 in full sun with LAI ≈ 4.5; a day is dropped when it has five or more bright-sun (above 400 W m−2) half-hours of release above 5 µmol m−2 s−1, and no other day meets this. Second, the 2005 soil-moisture record is treated as missing from DOY 165, when the 20 cm reading fell from 22 to 11 % and the 100 cm reading rose from 39 to 46 % within one day during a week with 50.6 mm of rain; this record is used only in the leaf-parameter comparison of Section 2.4.

2.3Calibration and validation

The design leaves one season out four times: the five cultivar coefficients of Table 2 are fitted on three seasons and the fourth is simulated with no further tuning. vLeaf is never fitted. The coefficients θ minimise a cost J made of root-mean-square errors, each divided by a typical error sk (Eq. 7), by differential evolution (SciPy; population 8 × 5, 30 generations, seed 3; 1,240 DSSAT runs per fold). All results in Section 3, on the poster and in the interactive model use two terms: silking date and grain yield (Eq. 8). Leaf area, GPP and ET are therefore never used in fitting and are independent tests of the coupled model. Section 3.1 compares this choice with eight other combinations of terms. G3 is fixed at 8.5 mg kernel−1 d−1 because only total grain is observed, so G2 and G3 cannot be separated. Management that was not recorded is held fixed in every fold: 7.5 plants m−2, 76 cm rows, nitrogen non-limiting, a water table at 1.5 m and 3 t ha−1 of soybean residue; sowing was on DOY 120, 109, 106 and 116, the last three farmer-reported [11].

Cost over a set of terms KJK(θ)=∑k∈KRMSEk(θ)sk,RMSEk=1Nk∑i=1Nk(mk,i(θ)−ok,i)2(7)
Cost used (silking + yield)J(θ)=RMSEsilk(θ)3d+RMSEyield(θ)0.10(8)

mk,i and ok,i are the simulated and observed values of term k in the three calibration seasons, pooled (Table 5). The silking residual is simulated minus reference silking day; the yield residual is relative, simulated ÷ farmer yield − 1, so syield = 0.10 is a 10 % error. Dividing by sk makes each term count about one at a typical error, so each target, not each data point, carries equal weight. A run that fails scores J = 1000.

2.4vLeaf leaf parameters

vLeaf uses the maize values of Drewry et al. [2] (Table 3); values Drewry et al. do not give come from von Caemmerer [3] or Srivastava et al. [12]. This set was chosen by comparing three published sets with vLeaf driven by measured tower weather and measured LAI, outside DSSAT (Figure 2). Choosing the best set inside each fold, from that fold's three calibration seasons only, selected Drewry et al. in all four folds, so the choice does not use the season being predicted.

3Results

In each held-out season the coupled model follows the shape of the mean diurnal GPP cycle, the seasonal course of daily GPP and the rise and plateau of LAI (Figure 3). Pooled over the four seasons, …. Predicted silking dates fall within 5 days of the reference dates and grain yields within −4 to +8 % of the farmer records (Figure 4, Table 4). Daily GPP is least well predicted in 2003 (R2 0.52), where simulated LAI peaks near 3.9 m2 m−2 against a measured 4.9 and simulated GPP stays high late in the season.

3.1Choice of calibration cost

To find which observations the calibration needs, the leave-one-season-out design of Section 2.3 was repeated with nine cost functions, each a different set of terms K in Eq. 7 (Table 5). Everything else was identical: the same coefficients and ranges, optimiser, seed, fixed vLeaf parameters and folds, 1,240 DSSAT runs per fold. With all five terms the run reproduces an earlier five-term calibration exactly. Every cost function is scored on the same held-out observations (Table 6, Figure 5); the full time series for each are in Figure 6.

Silking and yield are both needed. Without silking (costs 1, 2, 6) the held-out silking date is off by 13–16 days in some season, because nothing else pins down P1 and PHINT; with GPP alone (cost 3) timing is right but G2 is unconstrained (501–1062 across folds) and yield is up to 54 % low. Without yield (costs 2–4) the held-out yield is off by 17–54 % in some season. Silking and yield are enough: cost 5 matches or exceeds every other cost on every test, although leaf area, GPP and ET were never part of it. Adding LAI does not help (costs 6–8): it gives the best LAI R2 but lowers daily GPP R2 and worsens yield, because CERES-Maize starts leaf senescence at silking (Section 5) and fitting late-season LAI pulls the genetics away from timing and grain. Adding GPP to the other four terms (cost 9 against cost 8) recovers most of that loss. With four held-out seasons and three yield records, differences of a few hundredths in R2 between costs 5 and 9 are within what the data can resolve.

4Interactive model

Two tools let readers run the model. Section 4.1 changes leaf, cultivar and weather settings for a whole season through a surrogate of DSSAT-vLeaf trained on 10,000 DSSAT runs (Appendix A). Section 4.2 runs the exact vLeaf code, ported line by line from the Fortran used in DSSAT, for one day; on 400 test hours it reproduces the Fortran to within 0.0001 µmol m−2 s−1 of photosynthesis.

5Limitations

  1. Leaf ageing. vLeaf keeps full leaf capacity after silking, and CERES-Maize starts leaf senescence at silking, whereas the measured canopy stays green for about a month longer but loses photosynthetic capacity. Late-season GPP is therefore too high, most in 2003 (Figure 3).
  2. Generated hourly weather. DSSAT builds each hour from daily weather, so vLeaf never sees the tower's measured half-hours; part of the midday GPP error may come from this.
  3. Latent-heat timing. Driven by measured weather, every parameter set under-predicts morning and midday latent heat and over-predicts the late afternoon (Figure 2), which points at the energy balance or the closure correction rather than at the leaf parameters.
  4. Reference dates. Silking dates are derived, not observed; maturity is the end of canopy CO2 uptake; the 1999 sowing date is unverified.
  5. Unrecorded management. Plant density, nitrogen and the water table are assumptions; with the water table the crop is never water-limited.
  6. Surrogate. Section 4.1 is an emulator, valid only inside its input ranges and with the errors of Table A1.

6Conclusion

Replacing one step of CERES-Maize with a biochemical two-leaf model, with published leaf parameters and only five cultivar coefficients calibrated, produced a crop model that can be tested, and holds up, from half-hourly canopy photosynthesis to leaf area, silking and grain yield in seasons it never saw. The test also isolates what limits the coupled model now: the seasonal decline of leaf area and leaf capacity after silking, not leaf photosynthesis.

Appendix A. The DSSAT surrogate

The season model of Section 4.1 does not run DSSAT; it runs a neural-network surrogate trained on real DSSAT-vLeaf runs. General-purpose crop-model emulators are trained on very large simulation ensembles because they must cover many sites, soils, managements, cultivars and climates (for example the GGCMI Phase 2 emulators [13]). This surrogate answers a much narrower question, how one calibrated model of one field responds to nine settings, for which a few thousand runs suffice. Four properties of the problem make that so:

  1. One field. One site, one soil profile and one management, driven by the four observed weather years; the surrogate never has to learn how soils, managements or climates interact.
  2. Nine inputs in narrow ranges around the calibrated model (Figure A1a); the genetics ranges span the four independent calibrations with room on both sides.
  3. A few inputs dominate. … (Figure A6), so the effective dimension is well below nine.
  4. The error stops falling early. … (Figure A2).

The surrogate is checked against DSSAT rather than against itself: on an independent design of … runs never used in training or model selection (Figures A3, A5; Table A1) and on … one-at-a-time DSSAT sweeps (Figure A4). Its reference setting and the fold ticks in Figure A1 come from the earlier five-term calibration (cost 9 in Table 6); the silking + yield coefficients lie inside the same input ranges. It is valid only inside the input ranges, for this site, soil, management and the 1999–2005 weather; P2, G3, the stomatal intercept and the remaining vLeaf parameters are fixed, rainfall is not an input because the crop is never water-limited, and it predicts seasonal quantities and daily-resolution curves rather than hours.
